questions.text: How clearly defined is your target customer today?
questions.why: Knowing exactly who has the problem comes before everything else.

options.label: It is our own belief so far; we have not asked anyone outside the team
We have spoken to some people, but their answers do not yet point one way
We can name one specific customer group and state its problem in a sentence
Interviews with that group keep confirming the same problem

questions.text: How many in-depth conversations about the problem have you had with potential customers in the last 90 days?
questions.why: Recent, real conversations are the base of every customer claim. Pitches, friends, family and your host institution do not count.

options.label: None yet
A few (1 to 4)
Several (5 to 14)
Many (15 or more)

questions.text: Do your interviews show the same problem again and again?
questions.why: A problem heard once is an anecdote; heard repeatedly from one group, it is a finding.

options.label: We have not interviewed yet
Answers vary from person to person
A pattern is emerging but is not written up
The same problem recurs and is written up in an interview log

questions.text: Have you put a written offer in front of your target customers?
questions.why: Writing the offer down forces a clear statement of what the customer gets.

options.label: Not yet
We describe it verbally only
A written offer exists and has been shared with them

questions.text: Have people from your target group tried your concept or prototype?
questions.why: Showing a deck is not testing. Testing means a target user tried it and told you what happened.

options.label: Not outside the team, friends or family
Shown to target users; verbal reactions only
Tried by target users, with feedback recorded in writing
Tried by target users, and their feedback led to a change we can point to

questions.text: Has a named customer agreed in writing to a pilot or to buy?
questions.why: A signature costs the customer something; verbal interest does not.

options.label: No
Verbal interest only
A draft or an email of interest, not yet signed
Signed and dated by a named customer

questions.text: Have you and that customer agreed how success will be measured?
questions.why: A pilot without agreed measures cannot be shown to have worked.

options.label: We have no signed agreement yet
Agreement signed, but success measures are not agreed
Success measures are agreed with the customer in writing

questions.text: Do customers pay you today?
questions.why: Money moving is the firmest customer proof. Free pilots are not paying customers.

options.label: No paying customers and no committed pilot running
One customer has paid, or one committed pilot is running
A few (1 to 4) have paid, won through the same route more than once
Several or many (5 or more) are paying

questions.text: Can you forecast your upcoming sales?
questions.why: A pipeline shows whether wins so far are one-offs or part of a system.

options.label: No pipeline yet
Named prospects, each with a status and next step
The pipeline lets us forecast sales, and each new customer is onboarded with the same checklist

questions.text: Do existing customers stay, buy more, and refer others?
questions.why: Keeping customers matters as much as winning them.

options.label: Too early to tell
Some repeat purchases, not tracked
Retention is tracked, customers act as references, and new customers arrive without founders selling each deal

questions.text: What exists today?
questions.why: Be exact about the line between described, designed and built.

options.label: A described idea; nothing built
A written plan or design for the first build
A first build that works inconsistently
Core functions work in our own controlled tests
It has worked in conditions close to real use, outside our own bench or lab
It has worked in the customer's real setting with real users
It runs at commercial volume with support and maintenance

questions.text: Is there a written plan for what will be built first and how it will be tested?
questions.why: A plan specific enough to build from separates a design from a sketch.

options.label: No
A concept sketch only
A document specific enough to build from, with a test approach

questions.text: What testing has the build had?
questions.why: Founders who can describe failures know their product.

options.label: None yet
Tried informally by the team; nothing recorded
Tested in controlled conditions with measured results recorded
Re-tested across versions, with records showing fewer failures

questions.text: Have you measured the performance figure that matters most for your product?
questions.why: Every product has one or two figures that decide whether it is ready. You name it; the test report must report it.

options.label: We have not identified it yet
Identified, but not yet measured
Measured against a target in our own tests
Measured in field or customer conditions

questions.text: Has the build been changed because of test results?
questions.why: Changing the build in response to results shows the testing is real.

options.label: No
Changes made, but not yet re-tested
Changes made, and repeat tests show it failing less often

questions.text: Where has it been shown to work?
questions.why: Each step away from your own bench is stronger proof.

options.label: Only at the team's own desk or workshop
In our own lab or controlled setup
At a partner's or other external site, close to real use
In the customer's real setting with real users
Across several users or sites

questions.text: How consistent is performance across users or sites?
questions.why: One good result at one site does not show it will hold elsewhere.

options.label: Not in real use yet
In real use with one user or at one site
Consistent across several users or sites, with data

questions.text: Are volume, support and maintenance in place?
questions.why: At scale, the product is only as good as the support behind it.

options.label: Not applicable yet
Founders handle support case by case
It runs at commercial volume, with support and maintenance records

questions.text: Is it written down who pays, for what, and how the money is collected?
questions.why: User, payer and decision-maker are often different people.

options.label: We cannot say yet
We can say it, but it is not written down
It is written down

questions.text: What cost and price figures do you have?
questions.why: Estimates are a start; real figures are proof.

options.label: None yet
Written down, based on our own estimates
Calculated from real purchase or delivery figures

questions.text: Has your price been put to customers?
questions.why: However detailed the cost model, a price never put to a customer is untested.

options.label: Not shared with any customer yet
Shared in conversations; nothing changed as a result
Put to customers, and the price or model was adjusted from their response
Customers have paid or committed at the stated price

questions.text: Do you know your cost per unit and your margin?
questions.why: A business that loses money on each sale loses more as it grows.

options.label: Not worked out
Rough estimates only
Calculated from real purchase or delivery figures
Tracked over time, and steady as volume rises

questions.text: Have you chosen your routes to market?
questions.why: A long list of possible channels is not a plan.

options.label: Not yet
A general list of possible channels
Named channels, with steps and owners
At least one channel or partner is producing sales repeatedly

questions.text: Have customers paid or committed at your stated price in a pilot or test sale?
questions.why: Willingness to pay is shown by payment or signature, not by interest.

options.label: Not yet
A few (1 to 4) have paid or committed at that price
Sales come repeatedly through the same route

questions.text: Is there a written plan for delivering to customers?
questions.why: Selling is half the model; delivering at the promised cost is the other half.

options.label: No
A written delivery plan exists
Delivery stays steady as volume rises, with records

questions.text: Is there a written plan for growth, and are key figures reviewed?
questions.why: A model that keeps working is one that is watched.

options.label: Neither yet
A written plan for growth exists
Key figures are reviewed on a fixed schedule, and have been for some time

questions.text: Can you say what about your venture is hard to copy?
questions.why: This is wider than patents: secrets, data, know-how, brand, approvals and exclusive agreements all count.

options.label: We cannot say yet
We have a view, but it is not written down
Written down: what is new and who created it

questions.text: Have you checked what already exists: similar products, published work, existing rights?
questions.why: Finding a conflict late is far more costly than finding it now.

options.label: Not yet
Started; our own searches, with notes
The risk of infringing others' rights has been formally reviewed

questions.text: Is ownership settled between founders, any institution, and other contributors?
questions.why: University or employer involvement must be resolved in writing.

options.label: Not discussed
A verbal understanding only
Signed by all contributors and any institution involved

questions.text: Have you chosen how each asset will be protected: register it, keep it secret, or lock it in by contract?
questions.why: Different assets need different protection, and the reasons should be on paper.

options.label: Not yet
Chosen for some assets, but not written down
A written plan gives the route for each asset, with reasons

questions.text: Is protection being prepared?
questions.why: Preparation with professional help is what turns a plan into a filing or a contract.

options.label: Not started
We are preparing on our own, without professional help
Drafts are in progress with professional help

questions.text: Are records of what you create kept in a standard way, and is access controlled?
questions.why: Good records and confidentiality are what make secrets and know-how defensible.

options.label: No
Kept informally
Standard record-keeping is in use
Standard records, plus signed confidentiality agreements with those who have access

questions.text: What formal protection is in place?
questions.why: A filing or registration turns an intention into a dated asset.

options.label: None
A first filing or registration has been made
Extended to the markets and assets that matter commercially
Rights have been granted or registered

questions.text: How is your protected position linked to the business?
questions.why: Protection matters only if it earns or defends revenue.

options.label: Not linked yet
Tied to the business plan and to revenue
Licensing or partnership options built on it have been explored
It is monitored and renewed, and visibly earns value: licence income, exclusivity or a pricing advantage

questions.text: Who works on the venture today?
questions.why: This is the base for every other team answer. Use the conservative, named count.

options.label: One founder
One founder, in talks with possible co-founders or first team members
A core team; roles partly agreed and time commitment uneven
A core team where every role is written and owned

questions.text: Have you named the skills your team is missing?
questions.why: Knowing your gaps is worth more than appearing complete.

options.label: Not considered yet
We know them informally
A written list of gaps, including those that need advisers

questions.text: How does the team track progress?
questions.why: A steady rhythm beats occasional brilliance. A blank template is not a rhythm.

options.label: We meet when needed; no fixed rhythm
Regular catch-ups, nothing written down
Weekly goals and reviews, recorded for several consecutive weeks
The rhythm has been kept, with records, over many months

questions.text: Do you have active, independent advisers?
questions.why: Active means recent engagement. Relatives of founders do not count as independent.

options.label: None
Named, but little recent activity, or related to the founders
Independent advisers with recent, recorded activity

questions.text: Is there a hiring plan for your most pressing gap?
questions.why: A hire many months away does not close a pressing gap.

options.label: No plan
An informal idea of who we need
A written plan, with role and timing, for the most pressing gap
Hiring, onboarding and performance review run as documented processes

questions.text: Are founder ownership and decision rights agreed?
questions.why: Unsettled ownership between founders is a common cause of break-ups.

options.label: Not discussed
Discussed; nothing in writing
Drafted, not yet signed
A signed founder agreement, with decision rights recorded

questions.text: Are all critical functions covered, and is delivery predictable?
questions.why: Dependence on one founder for a critical function is a risk, whatever else is in place.

options.label: Some critical functions are uncovered
Covered, but delivery against plan is uneven
Covered by capable people, delivery tracked against plan, with structure beyond the founders

questions.text: Who runs the company day to day?
questions.why: An organisation is mature when it runs without its founders in every task.

options.label: The founders handle everything
Some areas run without the founders
A leadership team runs the company, with governance records

questions.text: Do you know how much money you need and how long your cash will last?
questions.why: What matters first is that a runway has been worked out at all.

options.label: No clear view yet
A single rough total
A budget showing monthly spend, cash in hand and months remaining

questions.text: What state is your funding pitch in?
questions.why: Grants count the same as investment; the pitch is what either funder reads first.

options.label: No pitch yet
An early or partial draft
Complete: problem, solution, market, traction, team and ask
Complete, and backed by a pack of supporting data

questions.text: Are your milestones defined and tied to amounts of money?
questions.why: Funders back milestones, not general growth.

options.label: Not defined
A list of milestones exists
Each milestone is tied to an amount

questions.text: Where are you with funders?
questions.why: A list of funders is a plan; a dated exchange is progress.

options.label: The route to money is not decided
A written plan names whom to approach; no contact yet
Live, dated exchanges with named funders

questions.text: Is your use of funds clear?
questions.why: A vague use of funds is the commonest reason a ready funder waits.

options.label: Not yet
A general description
A written use-of-funds statement

questions.text: Are the documents a funder would ask for ready?
questions.why: Being able to take money now means the paperwork already exists.

options.label: Not ready
Some are ready
The full set is ready to share

questions.text: What funding commitments do you have?
questions.why: Only commitments in writing, to this entity, are counted.

options.label: None
Verbal or soft interest only
A written commitment or term sheet is in progress, made to this entity
Funds have been received
We can choose between several offers or facilities

questions.text: How do you plan and control your finances?
questions.why: Controls and forecasting are what let a funder trust the next round to you.

options.label: No formal planning yet
The runway is planned against written commitments
Management accounts are kept and financial controls are working
Forecasts are checked against actual results, with governance over them
